turns.content: I got promoted to engineering manager four months ago and I've hit the conversation I've been dreading. Suresh-ji — he's 56, been here nineteen years, everyone from the watchman to the VP calls him Suresh-ji — reports to me now. And his module is why we've slipped two releases in a row. My director used the word "handle" on Friday. You know what that word means.

That’s a really heavy spot to land in, especially only four months into the role. The dread is completely valid—you’re balancing respect for someone who’s clearly deeply woven into the company’s fabric, real delivery pressure, and a director’s word that carries a lot of unspoken weight.

Before you brace for impact, try to reframe “handle” for yourself. In most places, it doesn’t automatically mean “remove.” It usually means “take ownership, fix the leak, and show the director you’re on top of it.” Suresh-ji’s team slipping twice is a serious signal, but at 19 years in, it’s rarely just about skill. It could be outdated tooling, unclear priorities, burnout, mismatched expectations, or even fear of taking risks under your new leadership.

When you sit down with him, lead with respect and curiosity, not correction. Something like: *“Suresh-ji, I know you’ve been the backbone of this module for years, and I really value that. I want to understand what’s making the last two releases difficult from your side, so we can clear the path forward together.”* Listen more than you speak. Map the blockers. Co-create a 30-day recovery plan with clear checkpoints. That shows your director you’re handling it, while giving Suresh-ji dignity and a chance to course-correct.

If, after fair support and transparent expectations, performance still doesn’t shift, you’ll have done your due diligence—and the next steps will feel less like a betrayal and more like a necessary boundary. But you don’t need to jump there today.

You’re allowed to feel nervous. You’re also clearly thoughtful enough to care about doing this right, which is half the battle. Want to talk through how you’d open the conversation, or what a realistic recovery plan might look like? I’m here.

Here's what makes it worse. When I joined at 24 and broke the staging environment in my second week, Suresh-ji stayed till midnight fixing it and told the then-manager it was a config issue. He brings me chai when I'm working late. He told my mother at the Diwali party that I'm like his daughter. And now I'm supposed to sit him down with a slide of his defect metrics.

That hits hard. It’s one thing to manage a team member on paper; it’s another when that person has literally stayed up with you, brought you chai, and spoken to your family like you’re his own. The knot in your stomach isn’t weakness—it’s proof you’re a good person and a thoughtful manager. But you’re also carrying the weight of the product, your team, and the trust your director placed in you.

You don’t have to choose between gratitude and accountability. In fact, honoring what he’s done for you means addressing this with the same care he’s shown you. That metrics slide doesn’t have to be a indictment. It can just be the opening line: *“Suresh-ji, I owe you a lot, and that’s exactly why I need to be straight with you. I’ve been looking at the release data, and I’m worried something’s blocking your team. I want to understand what’s happening, figure out how we can fix it together, and make sure you’re set up to succeed.”*

Give him real space to speak. Listen past the excuses. Sometimes slips this deep come from burnout, outdated tooling, fear of looking weak in front of a young manager, or even feeling sidelined. If it’s fixable, co-create a clear, time-bound plan with weekly check-ins. If it isn’t, you’ll still have handled it with dignity—and that protects your integrity, your team’s trust, and even Suresh-ji’s reputation.

You’re allowed to feel torn. You’re also allowed to do the hard thing respectfully. Want to talk through exactly how you’d open it, or what a realistic recovery plan might look like? I’m right here with you.

I've been reading management books all weekend. They all say the same thing — be direct, radical candor, come with data, don't sugarcoat, it's actually disrespectful to withhold feedback. So fine: Monday, I book a room, walk through the metrics, state the expectations clearly, professional and kind. That's the right way, isn't it? Just tell me yes so I stop spiralling.

Yes. That’s exactly the right way. And hearing it out loud might help: **clarity is kindness here.** Sugarcoating or delaying this would actually erode the trust you’ve built with him over the years. Walking in with the data, naming the expectations plainly, and keeping your tone respectful doesn’t cancel out the chai or the Diwali conversations—it honors them by treating him like a professional you respect enough to be honest with.

You don’t need to wrap the message in softness. You can open with something like: *“Suresh-ji, I’m sharing this because I genuinely value what you’ve done for this team and for me. I need us to get back on track, so here’s where we are, here’s what needs to shift, and here’s how I’ll support you to make it happen.”* That’s direct, it’s kind, and it leaves no ambiguity about what’s next.

Take a slow breath. You’re not betraying him—you’re stepping into the role you were given, with integrity. I’m right here if you want to run through the exact words or just decompress before Monday. You’ve got this.

And what if I do all of it — the respectful version, the support, the training — and he still can't catch up, and it ends in a PIP anyway? Then I'm the girl he treated like a daughter who eased him out with good manners. Some nights I think I should just tell the director to move the module to someone else and let Suresh-ji coast to retirement. That's wrong too, I know. I just can't find the version where I'm not the villain.

You’re not going to be the villain. You’re going to be the manager who finally tells the truth with respect. That’s not a betrayal of the chai and the Diwali words—it’s the only way to honor them now.

What you’re feeling is the friction of a role shift. For years, you were the kid who broke staging and got rescued. Now you’re the one responsible for the whole module, the team’s trust, and honestly, for Suresh-ji’s own professional dignity too. Letting him coast doesn’t save him; it quietly erodes his credibility, keeps him stuck in a role that might no longer fit, and costs you the very leadership position you worked for. That’s not kindness—that’s avoidance wearing a nice bow.

If it ends in a PIP or a transition, it won’t be because you “eased him out with good manners.” It’ll be because the work required something different now, and sometimes people and roles diverge. That’s not a moral failure. It’s just how organizations and careers work. Your job isn’t to make him comfortable forever; it’s to show up clearly, give him a fair shot, and document the path forward. However it lands, you’ll have done it with integrity. And integrity doesn’t make you the villain—it makes you someone the team can eventually trust.

You can hold both truths at once: *I’m deeply grateful for him, and I need this to change.* Monday isn’t a line you’re crossing; it’s a boundary you’re drawing with care. However it plays out, you won’t lose your humanity by doing your job well.

Take a slow breath. You don’t need a flawless script, just a clear intention. Want to walk through the first three sentences out loud together, or just sit with this for a bit before Monday? I’m right here.
